messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Clergy/Pastor
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Public Transport: Bus riding, Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
During the long years of displacement that defined her early adulthood, Amara crossed a border on foot as hundreds of others did. The journey was measured in the sweep of iron poles used as weapons against fleeing crowds, in the sharp lines of metal barriers, and in the sudden rushes of strangers. She had come to believe that the violence was woven into the very objects around her, and into the speed with which people moved. American by residence, her ethnicity African, Amara remains a clergy and pastor to her congregation. Yet the old journey persists in her daily rhythm. When the church bus pulls to the curb, she feels the familiar guard rise. A quick turn of the driver’s head, the sudden sway of a standing parishioner, the glint of a metal chair dragged across the parish hall floor—each of these moments pulls her attention. She watches others closely, reading their postures for signs that they might harm her, and she frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following. Her body holds the alertness of those early years, steady and unforced. The memories of that displacement do not arrive as quiet reflections; they force their way into her mind when she does not want them to. Sometimes, in the stillness of her study or during the middle of a sermon, she hears things in her head that she heard during the frightening event—the low hum of the camp generators, the metallic clatter of the barriers, the sharp shouts that cut through the air. What frightened her most was that the memory feels so extreme that it is hard to believe it actually happened to her. She touches the edge of her story, testing whether it is truly hers. Alongside this, she had come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it. If she thinks about the event, she will not be able to handle it, so she turns her mind away. She has learned to keep the thoughts at a distance, letting them settle without pulling them out for examination. Around this avoidance, she lives with a quiet sense of dehumanization. She feels like an object, not like a person, a vessel that has been moved rather than a woman whose interior life continues. To navigate the world, Amara adopted patterns that settled into habit. She wears concealing clothing, dark and loose, and avoids medical care, keeping doctors and therapists at arm’s length. She avoids talking, steering conversations away from the event and its aftermath; speaking of it brings the weight too close. Her occupation demands presence, and the church provides a specific environment in which these patterns are lived. During Sunday services, when she steps onto the platform or walks through the narrow aisles, her watchful gaze and the frequent checking behind her are visible. The bus riding required for parish visits, the visual alerts of weapons or objects used as weapons among the congregation, and the occasional dissociative feeling—all of these occur in the same space where she ministers. She dresses in concealing clothing and avoids medical care, she avoids talking and watches others closely, and the memories continue to rise and fall. Each of these experiences coexists in her routine, simply present. Now eighty, Amara sits at the threshold of a new decision. The accumulated quiet of her routines has become too heavy to sustain alone, and she has finally scheduled a consultation. What she is most hoping for is a space where the unfairness might be acknowledged without requiring her to retell the story, and where she might be seen as a person rather than an object passed from place to place. She was certain that the work ahead will not ask her to abandon her watchfulness, only to adjust its weight. What frightened her most was the fear that if she finally opens the door to help, the uncontrolled memories might pull her apart. Instead, she steps forward, ready to let the old journey rest beside her new life.
